stem: A pension scheme pays Rs 5,000 at the BEGINNING of each year for 4 years. The rate of interest is 10% per annum compounded annually. What is the present value of this annuity-due?  [Given: (1.1)^4 = 1.4641, so (1.1)^(-4) = 0.6830]

per_option_rationale.rationale: Using an incorrect discount factor of 0.7117 (from a wrong (1.1)^-4 approximation) gives approximately 5000 x 2.883 = 14,415, a computational error in the inverse power.
Computing ordinary-annuity PV (end-of-period payments) gives 5000 x (1-0.6830)/0.10 = 5000 x 3.170 = 15,850; this forgets to multiply by (1.1) for the annuity-due adjustment.
Simply multiplying Rs 5,000 by 4 without discounting gives Rs 20,000, ignoring the time value of money entirely.

explanation: An annuity-due has payments at the beginning of each period, so each payment is discounted one fewer period than the ordinary annuity. PV_due = PV_ordinary x (1+i). PV_ordinary = 5000 x (1-0.6830)/0.10 = 5000 x 3.17 = 15,850. PV_due = 15,850 x 1.10 = Rs 17,435.

explanation_sections.punchline: Annuity-due PV exceeds ordinary-annuity PV by a factor of (1+i) because every payment arrives one period earlier.
explanation_sections.lesson: Annuity-due = ordinary annuity x (1+i). Getting this wrong by omitting the (1+i) multiplier gives the ordinary annuity result (option 2 trap).
explanation_sections.timing: 85 seconds. Compute ordinary PV, then multiply by 1.1. Trap: option 2 is the ordinary-annuity answer.
